intro: Strauss’s Till Eulenspiegels lustige Streiche, Op. 28, follows Till as he rides through a market, impersonates a priest and makes fools of learned professors before the law catches up with him. The United States Navy Band plays it in Herb Weber’s transcription; a winding tune and a short laughing figure mark Till in each disguise.

sections.label: A · Opening in F major
sections.mNote: Till’s winding and laughing themes are introduced in the opening.

sections.label: B · Market scene, on horseback
sections.mNote: A cymbal crash starts the commotion.

sections.label: C · Priest’s tune in B♭ major
sections.mNote: A dignified tune interrupted by the rogue’s theme.

sections.label: Dev · Imitative episode in A minor
sections.mNote: Imitative phrases accumulate in the A minor episode.

sections.label: D · Held passage interrupting Till’s tune
sections.mNote: A quiet, held passage interrupts Till’s street tune.

sections.label: A′ · Till’s winding tune returns
sections.mNote: The tune returns and begins a further run of escapades.

sections.label: E · Trial scene, F minor
sections.mNote: A drum roll and heavy brass alternate with Till’s short phrases.

sections.label: Coda · Opening theme returns
sections.mNote: The opening music returns, followed by one last prank.

cues.title: Prologue in F major
cues.text: The work opens in F major. A winding tune introduces Till, and a shorter, sharper figure gives him his laugh. Both motifs return throughout the piece as Till goes from one scrape to the next.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey describes the prologue and two Till motifs. James Hepokoski, Framing Till Eulenspiegel, 19th-Century Music 30.1 (2006), discusses the opening F-major complex, bars 1–111. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two Till themes, horn and clarinet
cues.text: Strauss introduces Till with two themes. The first is a winding tune for horn, the second a short, clipped figure for clarinet. Both themes return later in altered forms, and their rhythms stay the same.
cues.evidence: Dotsey identifies the two themes and their original horn and clarinet scoring; Hepokoski discusses bars 6–20 and 46–49. This note describes Strauss’s themes, not a new instrumental entrance at this time.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Strauss on the work’s intentions
cues.text: Asked many years later whether Till had any “metaphysical” intentions, Strauss replied: “Oh, no—I only wanted to give the people in the concert hall a good laugh for once.”
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, quotes Strauss’s later answer to a question about metaphysical intentions in the piece. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/

cues.title: The Eulenspiegel stories
cues.text: The old Eulenspiegel stories send their rogue from town to town, where he upsets princes, clergy, craftsmen and scholars. The earliest surviving written accounts date from nearly two centuries after the fourteenth-century life assigned to him. Strauss gave him a new ending on the gallows.
cues.evidence: Dotsey distinguishes the legendary fourteenth-century biography, later written accounts and Strauss’s execution scene. Hepokoski, pp. 8–9, discusses the Volksbuch tradition and Till’s death in bed in the earlier tales.

cues.title: Ride through the market
cues.text: Till rides straight through the market women. Strauss marks the ride with a cymbal crash and flutter-tongued trumpets. A sudden pause follows, and Till escapes in his seven-league boots.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the cymbal crash, flutter-tongued trumpets and escape pause. The composer’s programme labels for bars 135 and 151 are reproduced in Hepokoski, Table 1, p. 13.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Pastor episode, B♭ major
cues.text: Till’s disguise as a priest is set to a B♭ major tune in paired phrases (bars 179–207). The short laughing figure recurs throughout. After a clarinet interruption the music darkens, and a fear motif sounds in muted brass.
cues.evidence: Hepokoski, pp. 24–25, analyses the B♭-major pastor episode, bars 179–207, including its paired phrases. Dotsey describes the clarinet interruption and the ensuing fear motif in muted brass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Till and the girls, bars 209–232
cues.text: Strauss’s own label for this scene is Till “exchanging dainty courtesies with pretty girls”. Solos for violin and woodwind accompany the flirtation. Till falls for one of the girls, and the music becomes more ardent as he woos her.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the violin and woodwind solos, Till’s infatuation and his wooing. Strauss’s labels 12–14 (bars 209–232) are listed in Hepokoski, Table 1, with Mary Whittall’s translations in note 23. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rebuff and vow of revenge
cues.text: The girl rejects him politely. Strauss’s label puns on the German idiom for a rebuff: “However fine, a basket still signifies refusal.” Till is furious; the orchestra cuts off, and four horns play his theme in unison as he vows revenge on all mankind.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the rebuff, Till’s fury and the four horns in unison. Strauss’s labels 15 and 17 (bars 244 and 263) are in Hepokoski, Table 1, with Whittall’s translations in note 23. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The professors, fugato in A minor
cues.text: The professors enter in A minor, played by bassoon and bass clarinet. Till puts his questions to them, and their answers form a fugato. One part starts a phrase, another imitates it, and further voices join.
cues.evidence: Strauss’s letter to Franz Wüllner, 20 October 1895, identifies the A-minor episode and fugato; quoted and discussed in Hepokoski, pp. 10–11 and 27. Dotsey describes the bassoon and bass-clarinet portrayal of the professors.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The “big grimace”, full orchestra
cues.text: Till sets the professors a few outrageous problems and leaves them baffled. From a distance he turns back for what Strauss labels a “big grimace”, a long, dissonant chord for the full orchestra.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the departure and the long dissonant chord. Strauss’s labels 19 and 20 (bars 315 and 345) are in Hepokoski, Table 1, with Whittall’s translations in note 23. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Till’s street tune, bars 375–382
cues.text: Strauss labelled this tune “Till’s street ditty”. It is a jaunty melody in the manner of an operetta by one of the other Strausses. The whistled tune soon stops, and a still, ominous passage follows.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the whistled tune and the ominous silence after it. Strauss’s label 21 (bars 375–382) is in Hepokoski, Table 1, with Whittall’s translation in note 23. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Franz Wüllner, 1895
cues.text: On 20 October 1895 Strauss wrote to the conductor Franz Wüllner: “This time let’s let these folks themselves crack the nuts that the rogue delivers to them.” Wüllner conducted the première in Cologne on 5 November.
cues.evidence: Strauss to Wüllner, 20 October 1895; James Hepokoski’s translation in Framing Till Eulenspiegel, pp. 10–11 and note 18. Première date on p. 4. https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf

cues.title: Return of Till’s horn theme
cues.text: After the quiet passage, Till’s theme returns. Earlier themes are combined as the tempo increases. The priest’s melody is drawn in and returns in D major just before the arrest.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the return of Till’s horn theme and the accelerated priest music. Hepokoski, pp. 33–37, traces the reprise from bar 429 and the priest theme’s D-major return at bars 567–572.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trial scene in F minor
cues.text: At bar 577 a drum roll begins the ff trial in F minor. The heavy brass play against short replies from Till’s theme, and the fear motif returns. The scene ends with the execution.
cues.evidence: Hepokoski, p. 37, identifies the drum roll and ff F-minor trial from bar 577. Dotsey describes the brass, Till’s replies, the returning fear motif and the execution.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hanging, bars 615–619
cues.text: The sentence is carried out. Strauss’s label in the score reads: “Up the ladder! There he swings, the air is squeezed out of him, a last jerk.” A strangled clarinet depicts the hanging.
cues.evidence: Dotsey identifies the strangled clarinet. Strauss’s label 26 (bars 615–619) is in Hepokoski, Table 1, in Whittall’s translation (note 23). https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Epilogue, bars 632–657
cues.text: In the epilogue (bars 632–657) the opening returns in F major, with a cadence in F major at bar 636. Strauss continues the phrase past the point where it originally broke off. Till’s motifs then interrupt for the final bars.
cues.evidence: Hepokoski, pp. 37–38, relates the epilogue at bars 632–657 to the opening and identifies the F-major cadence at bar 636. Dotsey describes the final interruption by Till’s motifs.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Cymbal crash into the market scene
transitions.how: Till’s tune breaks into short, quiet fragments. A cymbal crash starts the market scene at bar 135, with flutter-tongued trumpets among the rushing notes. Fragments of Till’s theme drive the passage forward.
transitions.evidence: Dotsey’s score account describes the quiet fragments, cymbal crash and trumpet effects. Hepokoski, Table 1, locates the ride at bar 135. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/

transitions.title: The priest’s tune in B♭ major
transitions.to: C · Priest’s tune in B♭ major
transitions.how: A gap follows the escape before the priest’s tune begins. The tune is set in measured, paired phrases in B♭ major (bars 179–194), marked gemächlich (at ease), and is accompanied by chords in the wind. Till’s laughing figure soon interrupts it.
transitions.evidence: Hepokoski, pp. 24–25, gives the B♭-major pastor episode, gemächlich and paired phrases in bars 179–194. Dotsey identifies clarinet and bassoons among the original score’s instruments and describes the motif’s interruption.

transitions.title: Return of the horn theme
transitions.from: D · Held passage interrupting Till’s tune
transitions.how: The quiet, held passage ends and the winding horn theme returns. Strauss brings back the F major and the quick, irregular phrases of the opening; Hepokoski places this return at bar 429. The theme passes between parts again, and a new crescendo begins at bar 449.
transitions.evidence: Dotsey identifies the still interlude and return of the signature horn theme. Hepokoski, pp. 33–35, maps the return at bar 429 to the opening, followed by the renewed crescendo from bar 449.

transitions.title: Drum roll and F minor trial
transitions.how: The priest’s tune is played in D major in bars 567–572. At bar 577 a diminished-seventh chord and a fortissimo drum roll cut across it, and the heavy F minor brass of the trial enters. Short, exposed fragments of Till’s music alternate with these brass statements.
transitions.evidence: Hepokoski, p. 37, describes D major in bars 567–572, the diminished-seventh chord, drum roll and F-minor trial at bar 577. Dotsey describes the brass statements and Till’s replies.

transitions.title: F major after the gallows
transitions.how: After the execution, six separated F major chords in bars 624–631 fall from piano to pianissimo. At bar 632 the opening phrase returns at half speed, marked Doppelt so langsam. It reaches an F major cadence at bar 636 and continues into the longer epilogue.
transitions.evidence: Hepokoski, pp. 37–38 and 40, identifies the six F-major impulses in bars 624–631, the epilogue at bar 632, its marking and the cadence at bar 636. The original string pizzicato is described here as separated chords for this band performance.

composer.epithet: Composer, the son of a horn player, who wrote long farewell songs for soprano.
facts: Munich, with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer; conducting with Hans von Bülow at Meiningen
Munich · Weimar · Berlin Court Opera, 1898–1918 · Vienna State Opera, 1919–24
Tone poems, fifteen operas, two horn concertos and more than two hundred songs
composer.background:
Richard Strauss grew up hearing the horn. His father Franz played in the Munich Court Orchestra, including the first performances of Wagner’s Tristan and Die Meistersinger, and detested the music. At home, Mozart was placed above every other composer, and Haydn and Beethoven were also approved. Richard, born in 1864, had piano lessons from the age of four and was composing at six. His mother Josepha came from the Pschorr brewing family. He studied privately with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer and learnt how an orchestra sounds from the players who worked beside his father.

Hans von Bülow took him to Meiningen in 1885. At twenty-one he had an orchestra of his own to rehearse, as well as a choir and a princess to teach. The violinist Alexander Ritter, married to Wagner’s niece, completed his conversion to the music his father disliked. Ritter also urged Liszt’s symphonic poems upon him. Strauss spent the next decade writing for the concert orchestra without voices.
